strategy_title: Masked Scalar Loads Slower Than Unmasked Indexed Loads
strategy_description: Replacing unmasked indexed scalar loads (using precomputed xindex with modular arithmetic) with explicitly masked scalar loads (using boundary mask guards on offs_m < M and offs_k < K) caused a 22% regression in kernel duration (30.88us → 37.79us). Although registers per thread slightly decreased (64 → 60) and dynamic shared memory halved (16KB → 8KB), warp cycles per issued instruction worsened (7.61 → 9.38) and memory throughput dropped (132 GB/s → 108 GB/s). The theoretical and achieved occupancy remained identical (50%, 6.25%), so the regression is attributable to the overhead of evaluating predicate masks on every load in the inner loop, which increases instruction latency and reduces scheduler eligibility (No Eligible: 86.86% → 89.35%). When the original kernel already handles boundary conditions implicitly via modular index arithmetic, adding explicit mask guards adds overhead without correctness benefit.
slow_pseudocode:
# AFTER (regressed): explicit masked loads
for k_idx in range(cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
    k_start = k_idx * BLOCK_K
    a_ptrs = A + offs_m[:,None] * 512 + (k_start + offs_k[None,:]) * 1
    mask_a = (offs_m[:,None] < M) & ((k_start + offs_k[None,:]) < K)
    a = tl.load(a_ptrs, mask=mask_a, other=0.0)
    b_ptrs = B + (k_start + offs_k[:,None]) * 1 + offs_n[None,:] * 512
    mask_b = ((k_start + offs_k[:,None]) < K) & (offs_n[None,:] < N)
    b = tl.load(b_ptrs, mask=mask_b, other=0.0)
    acc += tl.dot(a, b)
# Result: 60 regs/thread, 8KB smem/block, 37.79us
fast_pseudocode:
# BEFORE (faster): unmasked indexed loads with modular arithmetic
for k_idx in range(cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
    a_k_vals = offs_k[None,:] + k_idx * BLOCK_K
    xindex = a_k_vals + K * offs_a_m[:,None]
    a = tl.load(A + xindex)  # no mask
    b_k_vals = offs_k[:,None] + k_idx * BLOCK_K
    xindex = offs_b_n[None,:] + N * b_k_vals  # broadcast
    b = tl.load(B + broadcast_to(...))
    acc += tl.dot(a, b)
# Result: 64 regs/thread, 16KB smem/block, 30.88us
applicable_when: Never: this strategy caused regression. The anti-pattern is adding explicit boundary mask guards (offs_m < M, offs_k < K) to scalar loads in a Triton matmul inner loop when the original kernel already handles boundaries via modular index arithmetic or when the problem dimensions make out-of-bounds access impossible in practice.
do_not_apply_when: Do not replace unmasked indexed scalar loads with explicitly masked loads when: (1) the original kernel already handles boundary conditions implicitly, (2) the kernel is latency-bound with low occupancy (achieved occupancy ~6%), where predicate evaluation overhead per warp is amplified, (3) the inner loop is tight and mask computation adds non-trivial instruction count. The mask overhead increases warp cycles per instruction and reduces scheduler eligibility.
framework_notes: In Triton, tl.load with a mask= argument generates predicated loads that require evaluating the boolean tensor on every iteration. When the original code used tl.max_contiguous + tl.multiple_of hints with modular arithmetic (offs_a_m = rm % M), the compiler could optimize away boundary checks. Adding explicit masks removes this optimization opportunity and adds predicate computation overhead in the inner loop.

strategy_title: Adding num_stages Autotune Worsens MIO Stalls on Small Grid
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune sweeping num_stages=[1,2,3,4] alongside a B-matrix load layout change (from tl.trans(load([BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K])) to direct load([BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N])) caused a 22% regression in kernel duration (31.04us → 39.81us). Despite registers per thread decreasing (64 → 53) and theoretical occupancy slightly improving (50% → 56.25%), warp cycles per issued instruction worsened (7.62 → 10.44), scheduler No-Eligible increased (86.87% → 90.42%), and memory throughput dropped (131.81 → 102.74 GB/s). The achieved occupancy remained stuck at 6.25% regardless of the num_stages change, confirming the bottleneck is the severely under-sized grid (62 blocks on 132 SMs, 0.06 waves/SM) — software pipelining cannot hide latency when there is only one active warp per scheduler and no additional warps to interleave. The simultaneous B-load layout change likely disrupted the compiler's memory access pattern optimization, increasing effective MIO stall cycles.
applicable_when: Never for this kernel configuration: this strategy caused regression. The anti-pattern is expecting num_stages software pipelining to hide MIO/shared-memory latency when the grid is severely undersized (grid_size << sm_count, waves_per_sm < 0.1) and achieved occupancy is already at minimum (6.25%). Software pipelining requires multiple active warps to interleave; with only 1 active warp per scheduler, there is nothing to pipeline with.
do_not_apply_when: Do not apply num_stages autotune sweeps to hide MIO scoreboard stalls when: (1) achieved occupancy is already at the minimum possible given grid size (e.g., 6.25% with 62 blocks on 132 SMs), (2) active warps per scheduler is 1 — there are no additional warps to interleave with prefetched data, (3) the kernel is grid-limited (waves_per_sm < 0.1) rather than occupancy-limited by register/smem pressure. In these cases, software pipelining adds overhead (autotune cost, changed memory access patterns) without providing latency hiding benefit. The root cause (too few blocks) cannot be fixed by num_stages.
framework_notes: In Triton, num_stages controls the software pipeline depth for async memory operations (cp.async on Hopper). It is only effective when there are multiple active warps per scheduler to interleave. When achieved_occupancy equals the minimum dictated by grid_size/sm_count (not by register/smem limits), increasing num_stages cannot improve performance. Also note: changing the B-matrix load from tl.trans(load([BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K])) to direct load([BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N]) simultaneously altered the memory access pattern in a way that increased MIO stall cycles despite using fewer registers.

strategy_title: Expanding num_stages Autotune Range Regresses Small Latency-Bound Kernels
strategy_description: Extending the Triton autotune config list to include num_stages in {5,6,7,8} (alongside the original {2,3,4}) caused a 22% regression in kernel duration (31.04us → 37.63us). Despite the intent to hide MIO scoreboard stalls via deeper software pipelining, the winning autotuned config actually reduced dynamic shared memory per block (16KB → 8KB) and registers per thread (64 → 60), indicating the autotuner selected a lower-stage config — yet warp cycles per issued instruction worsened (7.62 → 9.30) and memory throughput dropped (131.81 → 108.71 GB/s). The profiling signals are nearly identical to the iteration-2 masked-load regression, strongly suggesting the code diff's introduction of explicit mask predicates (mask_a, mask_b) in the inner loop — not the num_stages change — is the actual causal regression, with the autotuner selecting a config that happens to use less shared memory. When a kernel is severely latency-bound with only 0.06 waves/SM and 6.25% achieved occupancy, adding more pipeline stages cannot compensate because there are not enough concurrent warps to fill the pipeline, and any accompanying code changes (e.g., masked loads) dominate the performance outcome.
slow_pseudocode:
# AFTER (regressed): expanded num_stages autotune + masked loads in inner loop
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=2),
    ...
    triton.Config({}, num_warps=8, num_stages=8),  # new high-stage configs
], key=[])
for k_idx in range(cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
    k_start = k_idx * BLOCK_K
    mask_a = (offs_m[:,None] < M) & ((k_start + offs_k[None,:]) < K)  # explicit mask
    a = tl.load(A + offs_m[:,None]*512 + (k_start+offs_k[None,:])*1, mask=mask_a, other=0.0)
    mask_b = ((k_start + offs_k[:,None]) < K) & (offs_n[None,:] < N)  # explicit mask
    b = tl.load(B + (k_start+offs_k[:,None])*1 + offs_n[None,:]*512, mask=mask_b, other=0.0)
    acc += tl.dot(a, b)
# Result: 60 regs/thread, 8KB smem/block, 37.63us, warp cycles/inst=9.30
fast_pseudocode:
# BEFORE (faster): original num_stages {2,3,4} + unmasked indexed loads
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=3),
    triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=4),
    triton.Config({}, num_warps=4, num_stages=2),
    triton.Config({}, num_warps=2, num_stages=3),
    triton.Config({}, num_warps=2, num_stages=4),
    triton.Config({}, num_warps=8, num_stages=3),
    triton.Config({}, num_warps=8, num_stages=4),
], key=[])
for k_idx in range(cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
    xindex = (offs_k[None,:] + k_idx*BLOCK_K) + K*offs_a_m[:,None]
    a = tl.load(A + xindex)  # no mask
    b = tl.load(B + broadcast_to(...))  # no mask
    acc += tl.dot(a, b)
# Result: 64 regs/thread, 16KB smem/block, 31.04us, warp cycles/inst=7.62
applicable_when: Never: this strategy caused regression. The anti-pattern is expanding the num_stages autotune range while simultaneously introducing explicit mask predicates in the inner loop. Even if the num_stages change alone were neutral, the masked loads dominate and cause regression.
do_not_apply_when: Do not expand num_stages autotune configs when: (1) the kernel is severely latency-bound with waves_per_sm < 0.1 and achieved occupancy ~6%, where pipeline depth cannot be exploited without more concurrent warps; (2) the code change is bundled with other modifications (e.g., masked loads, pointer arithmetic refactoring) that independently cause regression; (3) the dominant bottleneck is shared memory bank conflicts (12-way, 77%+ excessive wavefronts) rather than pure pipeline latency — bank conflicts serialize within each pipeline stage regardless of num_stages. On small grids (grid_size << sm_count), the fundamental occupancy ceiling prevents software pipelining from being effective.
framework_notes: In Triton, num_stages controls the depth of the software pipeline for async shared memory prefetch. Higher num_stages requires more shared memory per block (each stage buffers one tile of A and B). However, when the kernel is already severely underutilized (0.06 waves/SM), the autotuner may select a lower-stage config anyway, and any co-occurring code changes (masked loads, pointer arithmetic) dominate the measured outcome. The profiling signature after this change (60 regs, 8KB smem, 37.63us) is nearly identical to the iteration-2 masked-load regression (60 regs, 8KB smem, 37.79us), confirming the masked loads — not num_stages — are the causal regression.
